reading.body:
Every risk named here is physical: chips in transit, a Taiwan foundry, transformers, pumps, cleanrooms. None of it concerns models, data, or algorithms.

The ten items trace a single chain. It starts with rare earth export bottlenecks and foundry concentration in Taiwan, runs through packaging cleanrooms and custom silicon, continues into cargo cover on shipped accelerators and warranties on refurbished ones, and ends at the site with grid equipment and cooling. Two items are grid: transformer and switchgear lead times of two to four years, and delay in fibre trenching. Two are heat: thermal shock when cooling fails, and pump failure in direct to chip systems.

For AI this is a schedule problem rather than a cost problem. A logic flaw found after fabrication, a contamination event in a packaging plant, or a four year order queue for transformers all convert into time before capacity can run. Time is the input that governs how much training and inference is possible, and none of these delays can be bought down quickly.

The data does not say how often any of this happens, what it costs, or which operators carry it. Taiwan is the only geography named. It is a list of what can be insured, which reflects what operators expect to lose, not a record of losses. The presence of warranties on refurbished accelerators implies a secondary market but gives no measure of its size.
